  (`:567-568`). A stream past the 4 is dropped at accept (`:699-706`). A
  connection moves pools only when a reply says `authenticated: true`
  (`:834-849`). `HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT` is 5 s (`:570`), and the first
  request line has the same deadline. `IDLE_TIMEOUT` is 30 s (`:573`).
  The rate windows exist only for `/api/v1/pair` (6/min) and
  `/api/v1/info` (60/min) (`:583-587`, `Limits::limited` `:629-640`).

  frame. What this means for a page load: a browser opens several
  parallel connections and keeps them alive. Static GETs leave a
  connection in the unauthenticated pool for up to 30 s idle. A
  failed TLS handshake (the certificate warning) also holds a slot until
  it ends. **The pool of 4 is what an unpaired page load competes for.**
  Once paired, each fetch with the cookie or token moves its connection
  to the paired pool. The test `stalled_strangers_fill_their_own_pool_and_never_a_paired_clients`
  (`tests/remote.rs:3226`) is the existing model for that behaviour.
- The frame drain: `port.poll(DRAIN_PER_PASS)` then `serve_remote` for
  each (`src/app.rs:1585-1597`). The connection thread answers 429/503/504
  without the frame (`src/adapters/remote.rs:787-833`). Static bytes
  could be answered on the connection thread the same way (they need no
  core state), or on the frame through `serve_remote`. §4.1 "the frame
  does core state only" leans toward the connection thread. Not decided
  here.

### The router (`src/app.rs`)

- `serve_remote` (`:3017-3121`) refuses any path without the `/api/v1/`
  prefix with 404 `not_found` (`:3023-3025`). Then it answers `info` and
  `pair` unauthenticated (`:3027-3031`), authenticates, and handles
  `events` (`:3036-3038`) and the allowlist. The static paths would be a
  new arm before the prefix match, and they are the third thing served
  before pairing (§5's rule, `docs/remote-client.md` l.390 in the
  section, "Require pairing before anything but `/info` and `/pair`").
- `authenticate` (`:3125-3153`) knows only `request.bearer`. Both its
  refusals have the code `unauthorized`, with different messages: "pair
  this device first" (no token) and "the token is not known; pair again"
  (revoked, rotated, or never valid). **A page cannot tell "revoked"
  from "never paired" by the code.** With an HttpOnly cookie, the page
  cannot even see whether it holds a token. The "revoked" state in the
  issue needs either a distinct code (additive) or a non-secret marker
  the page keeps itself (for example, "I paired with server X as device
  Y").

  device. It does not check `Origin`. Neither does anything else.
- `remote_pair` (`:3606-3674`) compares the body's `spki_sha256` with the
  host's own, then the code, uppercased. It counts a failure on either
  (`PairingFailed`). It answers `{token, scope, server_id, device_id}` in
  the envelope. A cookie would be set here.
- `remote_info` (`:3568-3600`) carries `spki_sha256`, `server_name`,
  `capabilities`, `version`, `pairing_open`, but not the device's scope
  (it is unauthenticated). The header's "scope" comes from the `/pair`
  reply, and after that from nowhere: **no endpoint today tells a device
  its current scope**. A scope change in the dialog is invisible until a
  `control` command is refused. The Swift client has the same gap.
- `refuse` (`:3754-3772`) logs method and path, never the query. A
  `GET /?code=…` that reached the router would not log the code. Any
  new static handler must keep that true.

### The session list and the excerpt

- `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:636-688`) has `kind`, `card` (the
  card's word), `waiting`, `waiting_reason`, `liveness`,
  `trust_question`, `prompt_refusal`, `last_stop_at_ms`,
  `last_activity_ms`. **It has no excerpt or last-message field.** The
  §4.3 text (l.291 of the spec section) calls the card's one-line excerpt
  "`last_message` from the `Stop` hook on the record, a field of the
  session's metadata". That field is not on the wire, and `grep` finds no
  `last_message` in `control/src/lib.rs` or `src/app.rs`. The headset
  fills its compact card by fetching `sessions/{id}/last-response` per
  session (`client/Sources/SwitchboardUI/BrowserView.swift:149-163`). So
  either the page does the same (N requests and N watches, against a
  watch set capped at 128), or the issue's "No new read model unless the
  page cannot do without one" is tested right here.

  each, or `GET waiting` for the waiting set. That is what the headset
  does. Worker records are hidden unless `?scope=all` (`hide_workers`,
  `:3116-3118`).
- The session view: `last-response` for a Claude session, `screen`
  otherwise. Both are content keys that need `watch` frames on the
  socket for `changed` (§4.4 "Watch frames"). The page must speak
  `watch`/`unwatch`, wait for `watching`, then fetch.
- Reply box: `POST sessions/{id}/send` with `{op, text}` under `control`
  (`remote_command`, `:3159`). The page makes the op (needs
  `crypto.randomUUID`, which only exists in a secure context; see
  questions) and follows §4.5's `/ops/{op}` rule on a timeout.

### Pairing UI and the text paths

- QR payload: `src/ui/remote.rs:160-166`, a JSON object with
  `addresses` holding at most one `ip:port` from `remote::local_address()`
  (`src/adapters/remote.rs:962-970`, the outward route's source
  address). An IPv6 result would need brackets in a URL. The address is
  whatever the route picks, not necessarily the one the phone reaches.
- Swift: `PairingInvite.parse` decodes JSON only
  (`client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:93-116`).
  `switchboard-remote pair '<invite json>'` or `pair <host:port> <code>
  <spki>` (`client/Sources/switchboard-remote/main.swift:12-13,
  107-125`). `PairingInvite` is used by `ConnectionManager.swift`,
  `BrowserView.swift` and eight test files under `client/Tests`. Taking a
  URL means `parse` tries URL first (`URLComponents`, `code`/`key`/`id`)
  and JSON second. `addresses` comes from the URL's host and port.
- The README dev-aid text (l.265-278) documents "Copy invite" as the QR
  text and `switchboard-remote pair "$(pbpaste)"`. It must change with
  the payload.
- The script line `pairing <code>` (README l.278, `src/script.rs`) opens
  a window with a known code. That is enough to drive the page by hand
  against a test data dir.

- `tests/remote.rs` speaks raw HTTP/1.1 over a pinned rustls client
  (`http`, `:245-296`). It reads `Content-Length` only and keeps no other
  header, so header assertions (CSP, Cache-Control, Set-Cookie,
  Content-Type) need it to return headers. The relevant neighbours are
  `info_is_served_to_anyone_and_every_other_read_is_refused_unpaired`
  (`:426`), `the_allowlist_refuses_everything_else_with_no_side_effect`
  (`:682`), `pair_is_rate_limited_per_listener` (`:1406`),
  `subscribe_at` (`:1960`) and `the_client_fixtures_decode_on_both_sides`

- "Every path the page references is served" can be a test over the
  embedded strings. The page is plain JS with no runner in the tree, so
  its logic (query parse, `replaceState`, revision reconcile) is
  untested unless the plan adds a JS test harness, which the issue rules
  out as a dependency. The page's protocol logic is therefore checked
  only by hand.
- CI runs on Linux. `include_str!` of `web/*` is portable.

## Things the issue asserts that the tree contradicts or leaves open

- "Any path outside `/api/v1/` is refused": true (`src/app.rs:3023`), but
  on the frame, after the request was queued (so it costs inbox space),
  not at the connection thread.
- "the one-line excerpt the card shows" is not on the wire (above).
- "the device's scope in the header": no endpoint returns it after
  pairing (above).
- "'revoked' said plainly": the refusal code does not distinguish it
  (above).

  says. A page cannot read the TLS certificate it is talking over, so
  this proves only that the host *claims* that key. A relay forwards
  `/info` faithfully, and the host's own `spki_sha256` check in

  impostor's page under a relay. What it does catch is a genuine page on

  port, or a rotated key). The issue says roughly this. The tree adds

  browser, and the spec text must say so.

  on that host from receiving it. `localStorage` is per origin

  script on the origin can read it.

108	  `pair` unauthenticated (`:3027-3031`), authenticates, and handles
109	  `events` (`:3036-3038`) and the allowlist. The static paths would be a
110	  new arm before the prefix match, and they are the third thing served
111	  before pairing (§5's rule, `docs/remote-client.md` l.390 in the
112	  section, "Require pairing before anything but `/info` and `/pair`").
113	- `authenticate` (`:3125-3153`) knows only `request.bearer`. Both its
114	  refusals have the code `unauthorized`, with different messages: "pair
115	  this device first" (no token) and "the token is not known; pair again"
116	  (revoked, rotated, or never valid). **A page cannot tell "revoked"
117	  from "never paired" by the code.** With an HttpOnly cookie, the page
118	  cannot even see whether it holds a token. The "revoked" state in the
119	  issue needs either a distinct code (additive) or a non-secret marker
120	  the page keeps itself (for example, "I paired with server X as device
121	  Y").
122	- `remote_subscribe` (`:2723-2758`) requires `request.upgrade` and a
123	  device. It does not check `Origin`. Neither does anything else.
124	- `remote_pair` (`:3606-3674`) compares the body's `spki_sha256` with the
125	  host's own, then the code, uppercased. It counts a failure on either
126	  (`PairingFailed`). It answers `{token, scope, server_id, device_id}` in
127	  the envelope. A cookie would be set here.
128	- `remote_info` (`:3568-3600`) carries `spki_sha256`, `server_name`,
129	  `capabilities`, `version`, `pairing_open`, but not the device's scope
130	  (it is unauthenticated). The header's "scope" comes from the `/pair`
131	  reply, and after that from nowhere: **no endpoint today tells a device
132	  its current scope**. A scope change in the dialog is invisible until a
133	  `control` command is refused. The Swift client has the same gap.
134	- `refuse` (`:3754-3772`) logs method and path, never the query. A
135	  `GET /?code=…` that reached the router would not log the code. Any
136	  new static handler must keep that true.
137	
138	### The session list and the excerpt
139	
140	- `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:636-688`) has `kind`, `card` (the
141	  card's word), `waiting`, `waiting_reason`, `liveness`,
142	  `trust_question`, `prompt_refusal`, `last_stop_at_ms`,
143	  `last_activity_ms`. **It has no excerpt or last-message field.** The
144	  §4.3 text (l.291 of the spec section) calls the card's one-line excerpt
145	  "`last_message` from the `Stop` hook on the record, a field of the
146	  session's metadata". That field is not on the wire, and `grep` finds no
147	  `last_message` in `control/src/lib.rs` or `src/app.rs`. The headset
148	  fills its compact card by fetching `sessions/{id}/last-response` per
149	  session (`client/Sources/SwitchboardUI/BrowserView.swift:149-163`). So
150	  either the page does the same (N requests and N watches, against a
151	  watch set capped at 128), or the issue's "No new read model unless the
152	  page cannot do without one" is tested right here.
153	- Grouped by project: `GET projects` then `GET projects/{id}/sessions`
154	  each, or `GET waiting` for the waiting set. That is what the headset
155	  does. Worker records are hidden unless `?scope=all` (`hide_workers`,
156	  `:3116-3118`).
157	- The session view: `last-response` for a Claude session, `screen`
158	  otherwise. Both are content keys that need `watch` frames on the
159	  socket for `changed` (§4.4 "Watch frames"). The page must speak
160	  `watch`/`unwatch`, wait for `watching`, then fetch.
161	- Reply box: `POST sessions/{id}/send` with `{op, text}` under `control`
162	  (`remote_command`, `:3159`). The page makes the op (needs
163	  `crypto.randomUUID`, which only exists in a secure context; see
164	  questions) and follows §4.5's `/ops/{op}` rule on a timeout.
165	
166	### Pairing UI and the text paths
167	
168	- QR payload: `src/ui/remote.rs:160-166`, a JSON object with
169	  `addresses` holding at most one `ip:port` from `remote::local_address()`
170	  (`src/adapters/remote.rs:962-970`, the outward route's source
171	  address). An IPv6 result would need brackets in a URL. The address is
172	  whatever the route picks, not necessarily the one the phone reaches.
173	- Swift: `PairingInvite.parse` decodes JSON only
174	  (`client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:93-116`).
175	  `switchboard-remote pair '<invite json>'` or `pair <host:port> <code>
176	  <spki>` (`client/Sources/switchboard-remote/main.swift:12-13,
177	  107-125`). `PairingInvite` is used by `ConnectionManager.swift`,
178	  `BrowserView.swift` and eight test files under `client/Tests`. Taking a
179	  URL means `parse` tries URL first (`URLComponents`, `code`/`key`/`id`)
180	  and JSON second. `addresses` comes from the URL's host and port.
181	- The README dev-aid text (l.265-278) documents "Copy invite" as the QR
182	  text and `switchboard-remote pair "$(pbpaste)"`. It must change with
183	  the payload.
184	- The script line `pairing <code>` (README l.278, `src/script.rs`) opens
185	  a window with a known code. That is enough to drive the page by hand
186	  against a test data dir.
187	
188	### Tests that exist and what extends
189	
190	- `tests/remote.rs` speaks raw HTTP/1.1 over a pinned rustls client
191	  (`http`, `:245-296`). It reads `Content-Length` only and keeps no other
192	  header, so header assertions (CSP, Cache-Control, Set-Cookie,
193	  Content-Type) need it to return headers. The relevant neighbours are
194	  `info_is_served_to_anyone_and_every_other_read_is_refused_unpaired`
195	  (`:426`), `the_allowlist_refuses_everything_else_with_no_side_effect`
196	  (`:682`), `pair_is_rate_limited_per_listener` (`:1406`),
197	  `subscribe_at` (`:1960`) and `the_client_fixtures_decode_on_both_sides`
198	  (`:1829`, `client/Fixtures`).
199	- "Every path the page references is served" can be a test over the
200	  embedded strings. The page is plain JS with no runner in the tree, so
201	  its logic (query parse, `replaceState`, revision reconcile) is
202	  untested unless the plan adds a JS test harness, which the issue rules
203	  out as a dependency. The page's protocol logic is therefore checked
204	  only by hand.
205	- CI runs on Linux. `include_str!` of `web/*` is portable.
206	
207	## Things the issue asserts that the tree contradicts or leaves open
208	
209	- "Any path outside `/api/v1/` is refused": true (`src/app.rs:3023`), but
210	  on the frame, after the request was queued (so it costs inbox space),
211	  not at the connection thread.
212	- "the one-line excerpt the card shows" is not on the wire (above).
213	- "the device's scope in the header": no endpoint returns it after
214	  pairing (above).
215	- "'revoked' said plainly": the refusal code does not distinguish it
216	  (above).
217	- The `key` check in the page compares the URL's key with what `/info`
218	  says. A page cannot read the TLS certificate it is talking over, so
219	  this proves only that the host *claims* that key. A relay forwards
220	  `/info` faithfully, and the host's own `spki_sha256` check in
221	  `remote_pair` (`:3639-3647`) is fed by the page's body, which is the
222	  impostor's page under a relay. What it does catch is a genuine page on
223	  the wrong genuine host (a second installation at that address or
224	  port, or a rotated key). The issue says roughly this. The tree adds
225	  that §5's sentence "the host refuses a pairing whose `spki_sha256` is
226	  not its own, so a relayed request … fails" does not hold for a
227	  browser, and the spec text must say so.
228	- Cookies are scoped by host, not by port. Two Switchboard instances on
229	  one Mac (`SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT`, design §3.1) and any other HTTPS
230	  service on another port of that host would all receive a
231	  `Secure` cookie set by one of them. A cookie name per `server_id`
232	  avoids the clash between instances. It does not stop another service
233	  on that host from receiving it. `localStorage` is per origin
234	  (scheme, host and port), so it does not have this problem, but any
235	  script on the origin can read it.
236

The closest match is WebKit bug 41419, which is still open. Its reporter could not connect to wss:// servers using a self-signed certificate in Safari 5 or a WebKit nightly. Chrome connected fine with the same servers. Safari did not trust the certificate, and the connection only worked after the user set the certificate to "always trust." The bug asks for a certificate warning like the one Safari shows for HTTPS, or at least logging the failure reason. It was reported in 2010 and was still marked NEW when the page was last modified in January 2026.

Related reports suggest the problem is not limited to WebKit:

- An iOS write-up says self-signed certificates don't work for WebSocket connections. Accepting or manually installing the certificate didn't help. The workaround was a certificate signed by a locally created CA that the device fully trusts. The author also noted that this may need extra changes on newer iOS versions.
- Firefox bugs describe similar failures. In one, the user accepted the certificate for the HTTPS site, but the wss:// connection on another port still failed. Mozilla's own explanation is that an exception applies only to the specific scheme, host, and port that was accepted. The bug was closed as WONTFIX.
- A Qt forum thread reports the same "self-signed, untrusted" error, and a commenter there also called it an old WebKit issue.

I didn't find a WebKit bug that matches your exact wording, so bug 41419 is the best candidate. If your case involves a different port or host than the one where you accepted the certificate, the scheme-host-port scoping described in the Firefox reports may be the cause. Visiting the wss host directly and accepting the certificate, or using a CA-signed certificate, are the workarounds the reports describe.

Links: [{"title":"RFC 6265 - HTTP State Management Mechanism","url":"https://greenbytes.de/tech/webdav/rfc6265.html"},{"title":"RFC 6265: HTTP State Management Mechanism - Pike Programming Language","url":"https://pike.lysator.liu.se/docs/ietf/rfc/62/rfc6265.xml"},{"title":"RFC 6265 - HTTP State Management Mechanism 日本語訳","url":"https://tex2e.github.io/rfc-translater/html/rfc6265.html"},{"title":"VU#804060 - Cookies set via HTTP requests may be used to bypass HTTPS and reveal private information","url":"https://www.kb.cert.org/vuls/id/804060"},{"title":"Cookies: HTTP State Management Mechanism","url":"https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis.html"},{"title":"HTTP Cookies explained","url":"https://http.dev/cookies"},{"title":"Session data isolation and management","url":"https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/11431809"},{"title":"RFC 6265: HTTP State Management Mechanism","url":"https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc6265/"},{"title":"Session data isolation and management","url":"https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/10938915"},{"title":"Are HTTP cookies port specific ?","url":"https://www.wikitechy.com/interview-questions/cyber-security/are-http-cookies-port-specific/"}]

The search confirms that RFC 6265 explicitly says cookies are not isolated by port, and the newer draft keeps that position.

- **Section 8.5 (Weak Confidentiality):** The RFC's heading for this point is itself the claim you searched for. If a cookie is readable by a service running on one port, the cookie is also readable by a service running on another port of the same server. The same applies to writes: a cookie writable by a service on one port is also writable by a service on another port of the same server.
- **Recommendation:** The RFC advises servers not to run mutually distrusting services on different ports of one host while storing security-sensitive data in cookies (servers SHOULD NOT both run mutually distrusting services on different ports of the same host and use cookies to store security-sensitive information).
- **Contrast with browser policy:** Cookies for a host are shared across its ports, even though the usual "same-origin policy" used by web browsers isolates content retrieved via different ports.
- **Current draft:** The successor spec, RFC 6265bis, retains the same section. Ports are the only piece of the origin model that __Host- cookies continue to ignore.
- **Practical guidance:** One explainer suggests running untrusted applications on separate host names, rather than separate ports, keeps their cookies apart.

The search confirms that RFC 6265 explicitly says cookies are not isolated by port, and the newer draft keeps that position.

- **Section 8.5 (Weak Confidentiality):** The RFC's heading for this point is itself the claim you searched for. If a cookie is readable by a service running on one port, the cookie is also readable by a service running on another port of the same server. The same applies to writes: a cookie writable by a service on one port is also writable by a service on another port of the same server.
- **Recommendation:** The RFC advises servers not to run mutually distrusting services on different ports of one host while storing security-sensitive data in cookies (servers SHOULD NOT both run mutually distrusting services on different ports of the same host and use cookies to store security-sensitive information).
- **Contrast with browser policy:** Cookies for a host are shared across its ports, even though the usual "same-origin policy" used by web browsers isolates content retrieved via different ports.
- **Current draft:** The successor spec, RFC 6265bis, retains the same section. Ports are the only piece of the origin model that __Host- cookies continue to ignore.
- **Practical guidance:** One explainer suggests running untrusted applications on separate host names, rather than separate ports, keeps their cookies apart.

The official Apple article (support.apple.com/103769) sets out the core requirements. It applies to TLS server certificates and has four main parts:

- **Key size:** RSA keys for server certificates and issuing CAs must be at least 2048 bits. Smaller keys are no longer trusted for TLS. Certificates using RSA key sizes smaller than 2048 bits are no longer trusted for TLS.
- **Hash algorithm:** Signatures must come from the SHA-2 family, and SHA-1 signed certificates are no longer trusted for TLS. 
- **Subject Alternative Name:** The DNS name must appear in the SAN extension, and the CommonName is no longer used for this. 
- **EKU and validity (certificates issued after July 1, 2019):** Certificates need an EKU containing the id-kp-serverAuth OID, and their validity period must be 825 days or fewer, measured from the NotBefore and NotAfter fields. 

Failures are visible: connections to TLS servers violating these new requirements will fail in iOS 13 and macOS 10.15.

**Open question on private CAs:** Sources disagree on whether the 825-day limit covers certificates from user-added or private roots. One analysis says it applies to all TLS server certificates, including self-signed ones, and cites an Apple DTS engineer saying private roots must still stay under 825 days. Even your private or self-signed ones. Another notes that Apple's separate 398-day page says it will not affect certificates issued from user-added or administrator-added Root CAs. A third source points out that the 103769 article, which covers the 825-day rule, contains no such carve-out language. The primary Apple article supports the 825-day rule for all TLS server certificates, so I'd treat 825 days as the safe ceiling even for private CAs.

**Practical note:** The SAN requirement is commonly cited as the reason certificates that only set a CommonName stop working. The pfSense bug tracker mentions that the Subject Alternative Name requirements for TLS server certificates changed too.

The search turned up consistent answers for Chrome and Safari of that era: six connections per host over HTTP/1.1, though the sources vary in quality and age.

- **Direct match:** A Diffusion documentation page lists both Chrome and Safari at 6 maximum connections. It adds that the limit applies per browser, not per tab. Its table gives Chrome 6 and Safari 6 as the maximum connections. The page stresses that the cap is per browser rather than per tab.
- **Origin of the limit:** The same page ties the restriction to the HTTP specification, noting that the HTTP 1.1 protocol suggests single-user clients keep no more than two connections with any server or proxy. Browsers have exceeded that suggestion.
- **Corroboration:** A Blue Triangle article says Chrome has a limit of 6 connections per host name, and a max of 10 connections overall. A Medium post likewise lists Safari: 6 connections per domain.
- **Caveat on Safari:** A Tutorialspoint table lists Safari 7.0.1 at 6 per hostname, while a more recent Intellipaat table gives Safari "Latest" as 6-8. These are generic reference pages, so treat them as approximate rather than authoritative per-version figures. The Safari 6 figure of 6 is consistent across sources.

Overall, Chrome and Safari 6 each allowed 6 simultaneous HTTP/1.1 connections per host. Chrome also capped total connections at 10 across hosts. HTTP/2 multiplexing largely removes this bottleneck. I didn't find a primary Apple or Google source, so these figures rest on secondary documentation.

The search turned up no authoritative answer for bypassing the warning on an IP-based certificate that lacks a SAN, but several sources describe the relevant constraints and workarounds.

- **Apple's requirement:** Apple's rules say the server's DNS name must appear in the Subject Alternative Name extension, and CommonName-only names are no longer trusted (The DNS name of the server must be included in the Subject Alternative Name extension of the certificate.; DNS names in the CommonName of a certificate are no longer trusted.). A certificate with no SAN is therefore a poor fit for iOS.
- **IP addresses:** One Apple developer forum reply notes that a CA can issue a certificate for an IP address through the SAN extension (a CA can issue a certificate for an IP address via the Subject Alternate Name extension.). A Home Assistant thread reports that a certificate with the server's IP in the name worked, while a mismatched name did not (Safari or the iOS app doesn't recognize it as a valid certificate if the "common name" is not identical.).
- **Manual override:** An Apple forum post describes the warning dialog's Details option, which reveals a Trust control for that certificate, and says this stores the certificate without creating a profile (A dialog appears with the options "Continue", "Details" and "Cancel". If I click "Details", "Trust" appears in the top right. My understanding is that if I tap "Trust", the certificate is now stored on the device but a profile is not created.). A more recent post from iOS 26.2.1 users reports the Show Details button sometimes doing nothing, and suggests removing VPN or security apps and restarting the phone (If the Show Details / Visit this Website path is not working, remove any add-on VPN apps and any add-in security apps, force-restart the iPhone, and try again.).
- **Profile install:** The code-server docs say Safari will block WebSockets unless the certificate is installed as a profile on the device, and they describe installing it via Settings (Safari will prevent WebSocket connections unless the certificate is installed as a profile on the device.).
- **Practical fix:** The most consistent advice is to regenerate the certificate with an IP SAN (for example, using OpenSSL's subjectAltName config), then install and trust the CA on the device. One source notes that Apple's requirements also mean the certificate needs serverAuth in its ExtendedKeyUsage and a validity of 825 days or fewer (Certificates must contain an ExtendedKeyUsage (EKU) extension containing the id-kp-serverAuth OID. Certificates must have a validity period of 825 days or fewer.).

The sources are mostly community forum posts and dated Apple developer threads, so the exact button labels and behavior may vary by iOS version. The Apple developer posts are the most authoritative of the set.

(RFC 6455) - 0AndWild_log","url":"https://0andwild.com/en/posts/260210_websocket/"},{"title":"Websocket Protocol Explained","url":"https://adhdecode.com/debugging/websocket/websocket-protocol-explained/"},{"title":"rfc6455 websocket checklist","url":"https://glama.ai/mcp/servers/@shuji-bonji/rfcxml-mcp/blob/83092edb94a262a4fd63c5daabe5fb35de920066/examples/rfc6455-websocket-checklist.md"}]

The search turned up a clear answer on the RFC, with one conflicting source worth flagging.

- **Server side:** The server selects one or none of the acceptable protocols and echoes that value in its handshake to indicate that it has selected that protocol.
- **Client side:** RFC 6455 §4.1 says a client must fail the connection if the server names a subprotocol the client did not offer (the client MUST Fail the WebSocket Connection). This is the rule that applies to a server that echoes something unrequested.
- **Missing echo:** The RFC's introduction is stricter. It says that when the client requests a subprotocol, the server needs to include the same field and one of the selected subprotocol values in its response for the connection to be established. Other sources read it the same way. One notes that a failure occurs when the server doesn't respond with a valid Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header and the client requested one or more. A server-side example also states that browser clients which requested protocols will fail the handshake if none is returned (Browser clients that requested protocols will fail the handshake.).
- **Conflicting view:** A websocket-client library pull request argues the opposite, that omitting the header is harmless and that every browser WebSocket implementation treats that as a plain, successful connection. This contradicts the RFC's introduction and the browser behavior described elsewhere, so I'd treat that claim with caution.
- **Practical takeaway:** A server that receives a `new WebSocket(url, ['proto'])` request should echo one of the offered values, and should not echo a value that was not offered. A GitHub issue against a server library describes this exact failure, where a browser opening `new WebSocket(url, ['graphql-ws'])` failed because the server never echoed a selection.

The closest match is WebKit bug 41419, which is still open. Its reporter could not connect to wss:// servers using a self-signed certificate in Safari 5 or a WebKit nightly. Chrome connected fine with the same servers. Safari did not trust the certificate, and the connection only worked after the user set the certificate to "always trust." The bug asks for a certificate warning like the one Safari shows for HTTPS, or at least logging the failure reason. It was reported in 2010 and was still marked NEW when the page was last modified in January 2026.

Related reports suggest the problem is not limited to WebKit:

- An iOS write-up says self-signed certificates don't work for WebSocket connections. Accepting or manually installing the certificate didn't help. The workaround was a certificate signed by a locally created CA that the device fully trusts. The author also noted that this may need extra changes on newer iOS versions.
- Firefox bugs describe similar failures. In one, the user accepted the certificate for the HTTPS site, but the wss:// connection on another port still failed. Mozilla's own explanation is that an exception applies only to the specific scheme, host, and port that was accepted. The bug was closed as WONTFIX.
- A Qt forum thread reports the same "self-signed, untrusted" error, and a commenter there also called it an old WebKit issue.

I didn't find a WebKit bug that matches your exact wording, so bug 41419 is the best candidate. If your case involves a different port or host than the one where you accepted the certificate, the scheme-host-port scoping described in the Firefox reports may be the cause. Visiting the wss host directly and accepting the certificate, or using a CA-signed certificate, are the workarounds the reports describe.

Links: [{"title":"RFC 6265 - HTTP State Management Mechanism","url":"https://greenbytes.de/tech/webdav/rfc6265.html"},{"title":"RFC 6265: HTTP State Management Mechanism - Pike Programming Language","url":"https://pike.lysator.liu.se/docs/ietf/rfc/62/rfc6265.xml"},{"title":"RFC 6265 - HTTP State Management Mechanism 日本語訳","url":"https://tex2e.github.io/rfc-translater/html/rfc6265.html"},{"title":"VU#804060 - Cookies set via HTTP requests may be used to bypass HTTPS and reveal private information","url":"https://www.kb.cert.org/vuls/id/804060"},{"title":"Cookies: HTTP State Management Mechanism","url":"https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis.html"},{"title":"HTTP Cookies explained","url":"https://http.dev/cookies"},{"title":"Session data isolation and management","url":"https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/11431809"},{"title":"RFC 6265: HTTP State Management Mechanism","url":"https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc6265/"},{"title":"Session data isolation and management","url":"https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/10938915"},{"title":"Are HTTP cookies port specific ?","url":"https://www.wikitechy.com/interview-questions/cyber-security/are-http-cookies-port-specific/"}]

The search confirms that RFC 6265 explicitly says cookies are not isolated by port, and the newer draft keeps that position.

- **Section 8.5 (Weak Confidentiality):** The RFC's heading for this point is itself the claim you searched for. If a cookie is readable by a service running on one port, the cookie is also readable by a service running on another port of the same server. The same applies to writes: a cookie writable by a service on one port is also writable by a service on another port of the same server.
- **Recommendation:** The RFC advises servers not to run mutually distrusting services on different ports of one host while storing security-sensitive data in cookies (servers SHOULD NOT both run mutually distrusting services on different ports of the same host and use cookies to store security-sensitive information).
- **Contrast with browser policy:** Cookies for a host are shared across its ports, even though the usual "same-origin policy" used by web browsers isolates content retrieved via different ports.
- **Current draft:** The successor spec, RFC 6265bis, retains the same section. Ports are the only piece of the origin model that __Host- cookies continue to ignore.
- **Practical guidance:** One explainer suggests running untrusted applications on separate host names, rather than separate ports, keeps their cookies apart.

MDN says `crypto.randomUUID()` is limited to secure contexts. Its page marks the feature as available only in secure contexts (HTTPS), in some or all supporting browsers. It has been widely available since March 2022 and is available in Web Workers. These snippets came from search results, not the full MDN page.

In practice, a secure context means HTTPS or localhost. Plain HTTP on a LAN IP address fails: one report describes crypto.getRandomValues remains available in insecure contexts. Developers hit TypeError: crypto.randomUUID is not a function in that setup, and the usual fixes are HTTPS or testing on localhost.

One source conflicts with MDN. A Mironsoft article says On HTTP pages, crypto.randomUUID may still be present (this depends on the browser and its configuration). That is weaker than MDN's wording, so I'd treat MDN as authoritative.

For code that must run on non-secure origins, check `window.isSecureContext` or `typeof crypto.randomUUID` and fall back to `crypto.getRandomValues()`.

Links: [{"title":"Feature #9825: Requirements for trusted certificates in iOS 13 and macOS 10.15 - pfSense - pfSense bugtracker","url":"https://redmine.pfsense.org/issues/9825"},{"title":"Certificate Trust Store on iPhone, iPad, … - Apple Community","url":"https://discussions.apple.com/docs/DOC-250009603"},{"title":"Apple doesn't care who signed your certificate","url":"https://www.certkit.io/blog/apple-doesnt-care-who-signed-your-certificate"},{"title":"A Potential Open Letter to Apple about certificate handling in Safari","url":"https://gushi.medium.com/a-potential-open-letter-to-apple-about-certificate-handling-in-safari-080f7696fa68"},{"title":"How to configure development server certificates for iOS 13 and Mac clients","url":"https://jaanus.com/ios-13-certificates/"},{"title":"Validity period of HTTPS certificates issued from a user-added CA is essentially 2 years","url":"https://www.michalspacek.com/validity-period-of-https-certificates-issued-from-a-user-added-ca-is-essentially-2-years"},{"title":"Generating Self-Signed certificate for iOS 13 / macOS 10.15","url":"https://blog.lukaskukacka.com/ios/2020/09/10/ios13-macos1015-generating-self-signed-certificates"},{"title":"Certificate Requirements for Apple iOS 13 & macOS 10.15 - PKI Solutions","url":"https://www.pkisolutions.com/certificate-requirements-for-apple-ios-13-macos-10-15/"},{"title":"Requirements for trusted certificates in iOS 13 and macOS 10.15","url":"https://support.apple.com/103769"},{"title":"github.com","url":"https://github.com/syncthing/syncthing/issues/6036"}]

The official Apple article (support.apple.com/103769) sets out the core requirements. It applies to TLS server certificates and has four main parts:

- **Key size:** RSA keys for server certificates and issuing CAs must be at least 2048 bits. Smaller keys are no longer trusted for TLS. Certificates using RSA key sizes smaller than 2048 bits are no longer trusted for TLS.
- **Hash algorithm:** Signatures must come from the SHA-2 family, and SHA-1 signed certificates are no longer trusted for TLS. 
- **Subject Alternative Name:** The DNS name must appear in the SAN extension, and the CommonName is no longer used for this. 
- **EKU and validity (certificates issued after July 1, 2019):** Certificates need an EKU containing the id-kp-serverAuth OID, and their validity period must be 825 days or fewer, measured from the NotBefore and NotAfter fields. 

Failures are visible: connections to TLS servers violating these new requirements will fail in iOS 13 and macOS 10.15.

**Open question on private CAs:** Sources disagree on whether the 825-day limit covers certificates from user-added or private roots. One analysis says it applies to all TLS server certificates, including self-signed ones, and cites an Apple DTS engineer saying private roots must still stay under 825 days. Even your private or self-signed ones. Another notes that Apple's separate 398-day page says it will not affect certificates issued from user-added or administrator-added Root CAs. A third source points out that the 103769 article, which covers the 825-day rule, contains no such carve-out language. The primary Apple article supports the 825-day rule for all TLS server certificates, so I'd treat 825 days as the safe ceiling even for private CAs.

**Practical note:** The SAN requirement is commonly cited as the reason certificates that only set a CommonName stop working. The pfSense bug tracker mentions that the Subject Alternative Name requirements for TLS server certificates changed too.

The search turned up consistent answers for Chrome and Safari of that era: six connections per host over HTTP/1.1, though the sources vary in quality and age.

- **Direct match:** A Diffusion documentation page lists both Chrome and Safari at 6 maximum connections. It adds that the limit applies per browser, not per tab. Its table gives Chrome 6 and Safari 6 as the maximum connections. The page stresses that the cap is per browser rather than per tab.
- **Origin of the limit:** The same page ties the restriction to the HTTP specification, noting that the HTTP 1.1 protocol suggests single-user clients keep no more than two connections with any server or proxy. Browsers have exceeded that suggestion.
- **Corroboration:** A Blue Triangle article says Chrome has a limit of 6 connections per host name, and a max of 10 connections overall. A Medium post likewise lists Safari: 6 connections per domain.
- **Caveat on Safari:** A Tutorialspoint table lists Safari 7.0.1 at 6 per hostname, while a more recent Intellipaat table gives Safari "Latest" as 6-8. These are generic reference pages, so treat them as approximate rather than authoritative per-version figures. The Safari 6 figure of 6 is consistent across sources.

Overall, Chrome and Safari 6 each allowed 6 simultaneous HTTP/1.1 connections per host. Chrome also capped total connections at 10 across hosts. HTTP/2 multiplexing largely removes this bottleneck. I didn't find a primary Apple or Google source, so these figures rest on secondary documentation.

The search turned up no authoritative answer for bypassing the warning on an IP-based certificate that lacks a SAN, but several sources describe the relevant constraints and workarounds.

- **Apple's requirement:** Apple's rules say the server's DNS name must appear in the Subject Alternative Name extension, and CommonName-only names are no longer trusted (The DNS name of the server must be included in the Subject Alternative Name extension of the certificate.; DNS names in the CommonName of a certificate are no longer trusted.). A certificate with no SAN is therefore a poor fit for iOS.
- **IP addresses:** One Apple developer forum reply notes that a CA can issue a certificate for an IP address through the SAN extension (a CA can issue a certificate for an IP address via the Subject Alternate Name extension.). A Home Assistant thread reports that a certificate with the server's IP in the name worked, while a mismatched name did not (Safari or the iOS app doesn't recognize it as a valid certificate if the "common name" is not identical.).
- **Manual override:** An Apple forum post describes the warning dialog's Details option, which reveals a Trust control for that certificate, and says this stores the certificate without creating a profile (A dialog appears with the options "Continue", "Details" and "Cancel". If I click "Details", "Trust" appears in the top right. My understanding is that if I tap "Trust", the certificate is now stored on the device but a profile is not created.). A more recent post from iOS 26.2.1 users reports the Show Details button sometimes doing nothing, and suggests removing VPN or security apps and restarting the phone (If the Show Details / Visit this Website path is not working, remove any add-on VPN apps and any add-in security apps, force-restart the iPhone, and try again.).
- **Profile install:** The code-server docs say Safari will block WebSockets unless the certificate is installed as a profile on the device, and they describe installing it via Settings (Safari will prevent WebSocket connections unless the certificate is installed as a profile on the device.).
- **Practical fix:** The most consistent advice is to regenerate the certificate with an IP SAN (for example, using OpenSSL's subjectAltName config), then install and trust the CA on the device. One source notes that Apple's requirements also mean the certificate needs serverAuth in its ExtendedKeyUsage and a validity of 825 days or fewer (Certificates must contain an ExtendedKeyUsage (EKU) extension containing the id-kp-serverAuth OID. Certificates must have a validity period of 825 days or fewer.).

The sources are mostly community forum posts and dated Apple developer threads, so the exact button labels and behavior may vary by iOS version. The Apple developer posts are the most authoritative of the set.

(RFC 6455) - 0AndWild_log","url":"https://0andwild.com/en/posts/260210_websocket/"},{"title":"Websocket Protocol Explained","url":"https://adhdecode.com/debugging/websocket/websocket-protocol-explained/"},{"title":"rfc6455 websocket checklist","url":"https://glama.ai/mcp/servers/@shuji-bonji/rfcxml-mcp/blob/83092edb94a262a4fd63c5daabe5fb35de920066/examples/rfc6455-websocket-checklist.md"}]

The search turned up a clear answer on the RFC, with one conflicting source worth flagging.

- **Server side:** The server selects one or none of the acceptable protocols and echoes that value in its handshake to indicate that it has selected that protocol.
- **Client side:** RFC 6455 §4.1 says a client must fail the connection if the server names a subprotocol the client did not offer (the client MUST Fail the WebSocket Connection). This is the rule that applies to a server that echoes something unrequested.
- **Missing echo:** The RFC's introduction is stricter. It says that when the client requests a subprotocol, the server needs to include the same field and one of the selected subprotocol values in its response for the connection to be established. Other sources read it the same way. One notes that a failure occurs when the server doesn't respond with a valid Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header and the client requested one or more. A server-side example also states that browser clients which requested protocols will fail the handshake if none is returned (Browser clients that requested protocols will fail the handshake.).
- **Conflicting view:** A websocket-client library pull request argues the opposite, that omitting the header is harmless and that every browser WebSocket implementation treats that as a plain, successful connection. This contradicts the RFC's introduction and the browser behavior described elsewhere, so I'd treat that claim with caution.
- **Practical takeaway:** A server that receives a `new WebSocket(url, ['proto'])` request should echo one of the offered values, and should not echo a value that was not offered. A GitHub issue against a server library describes this exact failure, where a browser opening `new WebSocket(url, ['graphql-ws'])` failed because the server never echoed a selection.

**Title:** "We should log the reason when a secure wss WebSocket connection could not be established"

**Status:** NEW (Priority P2, Component: Web Inspector, unassigned)

**Date of last comment:** 2014-08-03, when the Radar WebKit Bug Importer added a link to rdar://problem/17898486. The bug was reported on 2010-06-30.

**Reporter's description (Martyn Loughran):**
Loughran could not connect to secure wss:// WebSocket servers from Safari 5 or the WebKit nightly, though the same servers worked in Chrome. Key sentences:

- "I have not been able to connect to a secure wss:// websocket servers using either Safari 5 or the WebKit nightly."
- "Nothing is logged in Safari or to Console.app, so I'm slightly at a loss how to debug further."

Later, in Comment 3, he confirmed the cause. Safari did not trust his self-signed certificate. Once he set Safari to always trust it, the connection worked. Key sentence: "The self signed certificate was not trusted by Safari."

He suggested either showing the same certificate warning Safari uses for HTTPS or, at minimum, logging the failure reason. Alexey Proskuryakov agreed that logging is the right approach and was wary of a bypassable warning sheet.

The results don't answer the specific question about IP-address hosts or self-signed certificates. None of the sources mention either case, so I can't confirm from them whether browsers accept Secure cookies there.

What the results do cover on the general rules:

- MDN describes the Secure attribute as limiting delivery to https: requests, with localhost as an exception. It also notes that plain http: pages cannot set Secure cookies. Indicates that the cookie is sent to the server only when a request is made with the https: scheme (except on localhost), and Insecure sites (http:) cannot set cookies with the Secure attribute.
- Wikipedia reports that Chrome 52 and higher and Firefox 52 and higher enforce this restriction against HTTP origins.
- The __Secure- and __Host- prefixes add browser-enforced rules. A __Host- cookie must have Secure, be set from HTTPS, omit Domain, and use Path=/ (per name starts with __Host-, the cookie must be Secure, must have Path=/, and must not have a Domain attribute).

For the IP-address and self-signed certificate question, a follow-up search aimed at browser behavior with self-signed certificates or IP-literal hosts (for example, Chrome or Firefox "Secure cookie IP address") would be the next step. Browsers generally treat a secure context based on the scheme and trust status, but I haven't verified that from these results.

The search didn't turn up any browser-by-browser comparison for Safari, Chrome, and Firefox. The results do cover the general behavior:

- **Same-site is not same-origin.** One GitHub issue reports that "Site" ignores ports, and browsers do not isolate cookies by port, so a page served from another port on the same host is same-site and gets the cookie. A `SameSite=Strict` cookie therefore won't block a sibling-port page, which matters if you rely on it as an origin check.
- **Cross-site iframes.** A separate GitHub report says browsers will not send that cookie on a WebSocket handshake initiated from a cross-site iframe, which caused a 1006 close in that app.
- **Cross-scheme navigation.** web.dev says that navigating between cross-scheme versions of a website (for example, linking from http://site.example to https://site.example) would previously allow SameSite=Strict cookies to be sent. This is now treated as a cross-site navigation which means SameSite=Strict cookies will be blocked.
- **Defense guidance.** OWASP says SameSite=Lax or Strict cookies prevent cross-site cookie transmission and strengthen CSWSH defenses. It also says the origin header should be validated on every handshake, which is a separate check from the cookie.

For your question about same-origin `wss` with a Strict cookie, the results imply the cookie is sent, but none of them tested that against Safari, Chrome, or Firefox specifically. You'd need to check browser-specific behavior directly, or look at the MDN SameSite and WebSocket pages, which weren't in these results.

The search didn't turn up a WebKit bug filed specifically for a SameSite cookie being omitted from a WebSocket handshake. It did surface several closely related reports.

- **Closest match:** A tldraw issue reports that a Safari WebSocket handshake was cross-site and sent no cookies, so session affinity failed. Safari blocks all third-party cookies by default (not just in private windows), and so does every iOS browser because they all use WebKit. A signed-in Safari session confirmed it: the WebSocket handshake is Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site and sends no request cookies.
- **Apple Developer Forums:** One developer saw cookies missing on a Safari WebSocket reconnect. The cookies were HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict, and removing the HttpOnly flag made Safari work as expected. No resolution is given in the result.
- **Solara:** Safari refused a Secure cookie set from http://localhost, which the thread links to https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=218980. Each websocket got a fresh session id, so popouts and reconnects failed, and the fix was a second, Lax cookie.
- **Related WebKit bugs on SameSite handling:** Bug 219650 covers cookies set with SameSite=Lax not being sent during redirects in Safari, and bug 255524 covers Safari 16.4 omitting the session cookie with SameSite=Lax from asset and fetch requests. Bug 198181 covers cookies with SameSite=None or SameSite=invalid treated as Strict.

To find the exact WebKit bug for the WebSocket case, search bugs.webkit.org for "WebSocket" together with "SameSite", or check whether the Apple Developer thread was ever resolved.

The accepted answer is short. It recommends avoiding in-app trust overrides, and the details on IP certificates and device setup come from other DTS replies in the same thread.

**Accepted answer**

On whether to remove the ATS stanza and install the certificate on the test device instead of handling `URLSessionDelegate`:

> "Yes. Writing code to override HTTPS server trust evaluation is extra work _and_ it carries with it significant security riks. If you can avoid doing so, you should."

**Bare IP address certificates (from the first DTS reply, not the accepted answer)**

> "Alternatively, a CA can issue a certificate for an IP address via the Subject Alternate Name extension."

The thread does not explicitly say that a certificate with only a bare IP and no SAN entry will be trusted. The SAN IP entry is the route DTS points to.

**What the user must do on the device (from the July 2017 DTS reply)**

> "I install the certificate authority's root certificate on my device (or simulator) per QA1948 [HTTPS and Test Servers]."

> "IMPORTANT On iOS 10.3 and later you have to explicitly enable the certificate authority in _Settings_ > _General_ > _About_ > _Certificate Trust Settings_."

**Other relevant points**

- Per the first DTS reply, the recommended setup is to "Create your own custom CA," use it to "create a digital identity for your server," and "Install that CA's root certificate on your client devices." Technote 2326 covers creating the test CA on macOS.
- For plain HTTP to an IP address, the first DTS reply says: "HTTP requests to an IP address will work without any ATS exceptions on iOS 10."
- The thread does not say whether macOS clients need the same steps. The Technote cited covers macOS certificate creation, and QA1948 covers all platforms.

**Resolution:** None is given. The thread has "Replies 0", and the poster asks whether the behavior is documented, but the page contains no answer or documentation link. The thread was created in June 2018 and has 2.8k views.

**Workaround implied by the post:** Removing `HttpOnly` makes Safari send the cookie, but that exposes it to script access, which the poster wants to avoid.

- **Hostname mismatch or untrusted issuer:** Safari's warning appears when the certificate doesn't list the hostname you typed or doesn't chain to a trusted authority. Show Details reveals which of these applies. (Source: tlsradar.com, item 7)
- **Self-signed certificates on .local names:** One Apple Community user found that a NAS with a self-signed certificate failed over HTTPS, and that the Show Details button sometimes did nothing. Their suggested fix was to check whether the certificate's hostname matches what they connect to. (Source: discussions.apple.com, item 5)
- **Trusting a development certificate:** One developer tool's guide reports that Safari showed "This Connection Is Not Private" until the root certificate was sent to the iPhone and trusted. After that, the .local name loaded without warnings. (Source: localcan.com, item 3)
- **Clock issues:** A wrong date or time on the device can make a valid certificate look expired, which can explain why it works on a Mac but not an iPhone. (Source: tlsradar.com, item 7)
- **.local itself:** Apple reserves .local for Bonjour and multicast DNS (RFC 6762), so a unicast DNS name ending in .local may not resolve on Apple devices. (Source: support.apple.com, item 6)

A practical path is to use a certificate that covers the exact hostname (for example, mac.local), install and trust its root CA on the iPhone, and confirm the device clock is correct. Note that "Mac.local" is a hostname, so it should match the certificate's name case-insensitively. I didn't find a source confirming that Safari's behavior differs from macOS Safari for this case; one source says the warnings are identical and share the same trust store. The search turned up a known iOS 18 bug and a standard workaround, but nothing that directly addresses a leaf certificate.

**Likely cause: an iOS 18 bug, fixed in later betas.** Several developer forum threads describe self-signed roots failing to appear in Certificate Trust Settings after installing a profile. One thread says the same certificate worked on iOS 16.7.10 and 17.6.1 but not on iOS 18.0 (Same cert and processes work on iOS 16.7.10, iOS 17.6.1 and iPadOS 18.0). A DTS engineer reported that after upgrading to iOS 18.2 b4, I can finally see the missing certificates in the Certificate Trust Settings. A related report says the problem appeared after migrating from iOS 16 or earlier, not on devices that upgraded from iOS 17 (the certificate does not appear in the Certificate Trust Settings (Full Trust for Root Certificates) list. However, the same certificate can be successfully installed on an iOS 18 device that hasn't gone through migration).

**Standard steps.** Apple's guidance is that a manually installed certificate profile is not automatically trusted for SSL. Trust must be enabled separately (go to Settings > General > About > Certificate Trust Settings. Under "Enable full trust for root certificates," turn on trust for the certificate.). Another user reports that the certificate only appears in that list after installing it from VPN & Device Management (tap on your certificate. Then tap on "Install" in the upper-right corner, and agree to the warning. Once you have done that, you can go to Settings->General->About->Certificate Trust Settings, and the certificate should be there).

**Leaf vs. CA certificate.** One answer says the trust relies on the issuing CA, not the server certificate: the key here is that you need to use the CA certificate and not the server certificate, so that the iPhone will trust the entire certificate chain. If only the leaf is installed, the profile may show as "Not Verified" and the trust toggle may never appear. Installing the root or CA certificate is therefore the usual fix. Note that this is a forum answer rather than official documentation, and I did not find a source confirming that a leaf-only profile never shows in the list.

**Practical next steps:**
- Confirm the device's iOS version. If it's iOS 18.0 or 18.1 and the device was migrated, updating to 18.2 or later may resolve the missing entry.
- Install the CA or root certificate, not just the server leaf, then check Certificate Trust Settings.
- Some users reported that resetting all settings restored the list, though one said it was a workaround rather than a confirmed fix.

results:
The search turned up a known iOS 18 bug and a standard workaround, but nothing that directly addresses a leaf certificate.

**Likely cause: an iOS 18 bug, fixed in later betas.** Several developer forum threads describe self-signed roots failing to appear in Certificate Trust Settings after installing a profile. One thread says the same certificate worked on iOS 16.7.10 and 17.6.1 but not on iOS 18.0 (Same cert and processes work on iOS 16.7.10, iOS 17.6.1 and iPadOS 18.0). A DTS engineer reported that after upgrading to iOS 18.2 b4, I can finally see the missing certificates in the Certificate Trust Settings. A related report says the problem appeared after migrating from iOS 16 or earlier, not on devices that upgraded from iOS 17 (the certificate does not appear in the Certificate Trust Settings (Full Trust for Root Certificates) list. However, the same certificate can be successfully installed on an iOS 18 device that hasn't gone through migration).

**Standard steps.** Apple's guidance is that a manually installed certificate profile is not automatically trusted for SSL. Trust must be enabled separately (go to Settings > General > About > Certificate Trust Settings. Under "Enable full trust for root certificates," turn on trust for the certificate.). Another user reports that the certificate only appears in that list after installing it from VPN & Device Management (tap on your certificate. Then tap on "Install" in the upper-right corner, and agree to the warning. Once you have done that, you can go to Settings->General->About->Certificate Trust Settings, and the certificate should be there).

**Leaf vs. CA certificate.** One answer says the trust relies on the issuing CA, not the server certificate: the key here is that you need to use the CA certificate and not the server certificate, so that the iPhone will trust the entire certificate chain. If only the leaf is installed, the profile may show as "Not Verified" and the trust toggle may never appear. Installing the root or CA certificate is therefore the usual fix. Note that this is a forum answer rather than official documentation, and I did not find a source confirming that a leaf-only profile never shows in the list.

**Practical next steps:**
- Confirm the device's iOS version. If it's iOS 18.0 or 18.1 and the device was migrated, updating to 18.2 or later may resolve the missing entry.
- Install the CA or root certificate, not just the server leaf, then check Certificate Trust Settings.
- Some users reported that resetting all settings restored the list, though one said it was a workaround rather than a confirmed fix.

The search confirms that MDN describes `replaceState()` as changing the current history entry rather than adding one, with some nuances:

- **Core behavior:** MDN's reference page says the method modifies the current history entry, replacing it with the state object and URL passed in the method parameters. The "Working with the History API" guide frames it as operating exactly like history.pushState(), except that replaceState() modifies the current history entry instead of creating a new one.
- **Caveat:** That same guide adds that this doesn't prevent the creation of a new entry in the global browser history. So the change is scoped to the site's session history, not the browser's overall history.
- **Typical use:** MDN notes it is particularly useful when you want to update the state object or URL of the current history entry in response to some user action.
- **Constraint:** The new URL must share the current origin, and the method throws otherwise (The new URL must be of the same origin as the current URL; otherwise the replaceState() method throws an exception.).
- **Source discrepancy:** One third-party article (xjavascript.com) gives a worked example implying the replaced entry disappears from back-button navigation. That conflicts with MDN's description, so I'd rely on MDN and treat that example with caution.

The MDN pages were the most authoritative results. The first MDN-mirror result was an older copy, but its wording matches the current page.

# Facts for issue #230 (browser page on the remote port)

No spike. Every question that turns on Safari or iOS behaviour needs a device, and a Chrome or headless run would answer a neighbouring question. Queries are Qn, fetches Fn, listed at the end.

## Settled

Tree (this worktree, 7fe8949):
- The card excerpt is a UI cache, not on the wire or in the record. Captions live in `ui_state.captions`, filled from the transcript (src/app.rs:888-898, 1184-1185; `caption_of` at :4104). No `last_message` or excerpt field in `control/src/lib.rs` or `src/app.rs` (grep). The plan adds an app-layer read-model field, or fetches `last-response` per card as the headset does.
- `make_identity` always generates a new key (src/adapters/remote.rs:95-101), and the key PEM is saved to the secrets store (src/app.rs:2866-2871). A reissue over the same key is therefore possible. rcgen 0.14.10 (Cargo.lock:4034-4035) has `KeyPair::from_pem` (F11). The SAN and validity fields of `CertificateParams` were not checked.
- The current certificate has a CN and no SAN (src/adapters/remote.rs:101, 103-106) and sets no EKU. It fails Apple's SAN and EKU rules (F1). Its validity was not checked against rcgen's defaults, so the notes' year-4096 claim is unverified.
- Every reply is written with `Content-Type: application/json` and `Connection: keep-alive` (src/adapters/remote.rs:530-552, :545). The listener reads no `Cookie`, `Origin` or `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` (grep of src/adapters/remote.rs and src/app.rs, which finds none).
- No literal `RemoteRequest {` exists in `src/` or `tests/` (grep), so new request fields touch no construction site.
- `MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED = 4` (src/adapters/remote.rs:567), enforced at accept (:702).
- Watches with subscribers survive eviction when the set is over `WATCH_CAP` = 128 (src/content.rs:42; src/app.rs:1787-1789). A page's watches cannot push out a headset's live watch. `WATCH_IDLE` is 60 s (src/content.rs:40).

Standards and vendor documents:
- Apple: TLS server certificates issued after 1 July 2019 need a DNS name in SAN (CN is not trusted), an EKU with serverAuth, and validity of 825 days or fewer (F1, Q2). Whether this applies to self-signed or user-trusted roots is not stated (see Unresolved). The plan builds a reissue that meets all three either way.
- A manually installed root is trusted only after Settings > General > About > Certificate Trust Settings > "Enable full trust for root certificates" is switched on (F12).
- WebKit bug 41419 is open (status NEW; reported 2010 against Safari 5; last vendor-side entry a 2014 Radar import). It reports that a self-signed `wss://` server is refused until the owner sets "always trust", after which it connects (F2, Q3). No source contradicts it. It is one report on an old Safari, so current iOS is untested.
- RFC 6455 §4.2.2: the server echoes one offered subprotocol or none (steps 4, 5.5). §4.1 item 6: a client must fail a response naming a protocol it did not offer (F4). The plan echoes exactly one offered value.
- WHATWG WebSocket: every requested protocol is combined into the handshake's `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` header (F7).
- RFC 6265 §8.5: cookies do not isolate by port, and servers SHOULD NOT run mutually distrusting services on different ports of one host while storing security-sensitive data in cookies (F3, Q5).
- W3C Secure Contexts §3.1 step 3: an `https` origin is potentially trustworthy by scheme. The text does not mention certificate errors, so per the spec a click-through page is a secure context (F6). Browser behaviour is not checked here.
- MDN: `crypto.randomUUID()` is available only in secure contexts (F5, Q7).
- OWASP WebSocket cheat sheet: validate `Origin` on every handshake; browsers include cookies in WebSocket handshakes, which makes cross-site hijacking possible (F9). RFC 6455 §10.2 was not read.
- MDN: `replaceState()` replaces the current session-history entry and requires the same origin (Q15). It does not reach browser-wide history (see Unresolved).

## Unresolved

U1. Does iOS Safari carry a click-through for `wss://` to a self-signed certificate? Tried Q1, Q3, F2. Bug 41419 is about an old Safari, and the wider searches found only forum posts. Build to: the page does not depend on the WebSocket. When the socket fails it polls `GET` for the revision, and the trust step in O1 is offered.

U2. Does iOS trust a self-signed leaf installed by profile once its full-trust switch is on? Tried Q14. Results are forum answers, plus iOS 18 threads reporting private roots missing from the list (Apple forum thread 764673, not fetched). F12 covers roots only. Build to: the reissued certificate, with the trust step optional until a device run. If the leaf does not show, a local CA is needed (O3).

U3. Connections per host that a browser opens for the page load. Tried Q6. Sources are secondary (Diffusion docs; Blue Triangle): six per host for Chrome and Safari of that era. Current iOS Safari is unknown. Build to: assume at least six. Static `GET`s must not let the page load hold all four unauthenticated slots (src/adapters/remote.rs:567, :702). Either the static paths get their own pool, or they are answered without taking a pool slot.

U4. Does Safari send a `SameSite=Strict` cookie on a same-origin `wss://` handshake? Tried Q8, Q10, F10. Apple forum thread 104488 (June 2018, no reply) reports that Safari omits HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict cookies on the second `wss` handshake, and that removing HttpOnly fixes it. A tldraw issue (Q10) shows a cross-site Safari handshake sends no cookies, which is a different case. Build to: the plan does not rely on a cookie for the WebSocket until a device run passes. The subprotocol path does not depend on this.

U5. Does a click-through survive reloads, launches and an IP change? Tried Q11: no source found. Build to: the page treats the warning as present on every visit and does not assume the exception persists.

U6. Does a click-through page keep `isSecureContext` true, and do Secure cookies stick, in iOS Safari? The spec says yes (F6); no browser check. Build to: use `randomUUID` only if the device run shows `isSecureContext` true.

U7. Does `<name>.local` resolve and get a trusted certificate in iOS Safari? Tried Q12. Apple support 101903 (lead) warns that `.local` may not resolve through unicast DNS. Build to: the IP-only URL. `.local` is out of the first cut.

U8. Does the URL with the code reach browser-wide history, "recently closed" or tab sync before `replaceState` runs? Tried Q15, which covers session history only. Build to: the plan may claim only that the session entry is replaced.

U9. Do Chrome, Firefox and Safari keep a `Secure` cookie set by an https response with an untrusted certificate, on an IP-literal host? Tried Q9: search snippets only (MDN's Secure rule; Chrome and Firefox 52). Build to: the cookie name carries the `server_id` (U-via RFC 6265 §8.5), and the device run decides.

U10. RFC 6455 handshake when a protocol was requested but none is echoed: Q4 turned up a claim that browsers fail and a conflicting client PR. Build to: always echo, which satisfies both readings.

## For the owner

O1. Trust (decision 1). The click-through may not carry the WebSocket (U1). Option A: add a pre-pairing download of the public certificate, and the owner installs it and switches on full trust on the device. Option B: no install step; the page works by polling if the socket is refused. Both branches work if the plan builds the reissue and the polling fallback. Recommend: build both, and say in the paired-devices dialog which one the owner used.

O2. Token transport (decision 2). The cookie works only if U4 passes on a device. The subprotocol token works either way, but keeps the token in page storage, where a script on the origin can read it. Both branches work if the plan builds the subprotocol path; the cookie is added only on a pass.

O3. Local CA (only if U2 fails). A CA key in the Keychain, with the leaf signed by it, lets the owner trust a root with the switch that Apple documents. Yes or no?

O4. Origins to accept on the WebSocket and POSTs (decision 5). Option A: exactly `https://<address>:<port>` as the host advertises it. Option B: also `localhost` on the same port. Both work with the origin check; the choice decides which browsers reach a host by name.

O5. Who reissues the certificate when the route address changes (U5 and the reissue)? Option A: at pairing-window open, if the address differs. Option B: at startup only. Both work; A leaves the trust step to the owner each time.

## Queries and fetches

Queries (WebSearch, standard mode unless noted):
- Q1 "iOS Safari proceed past self-signed certificate warning IP address no subjectAltName"
- Q2 "Apple requirements for trusted certificates in iOS 13 and macOS 10.15 subjectAltName 825 days"
- Q3 "WebKit WebSocket wss self-signed certificate exception not applied bug"
- Q4 "RFC 6455 Sec-WebSocket-Protocol server selects subprotocol browser fails handshake if not echoed"
- Q5 "RFC 6265 cookies do not provide isolation by port"
- Q6 "browser maximum simultaneous HTTP/1.1 connections per host Chrome Safari 6"
- Q7 "MDN crypto.randomUUID secure context availability"
- Q8 "SameSite=Strict cookie sent with WebSocket handshake same-origin wss Safari Chrome Firefox"
- Q9 "Secure cookie over HTTPS IP address host allowed Set-Cookie Secure self-signed"
- Q10 "WebKit bug SameSite cookie not sent WebSocket handshake Safari"
- Q11 "Safari remembers accepted self-signed certificate exception Show Details visit website how long persists iOS"
- Q12 "iOS Safari open https://Mac.local hostname Bonjour .local resolve certificate warning"
- Q14 "iOS install self-signed server certificate profile not listed Certificate Trust Settings leaf certificate trust"
- Q15 "MDN History replaceState() modifies the current history entry instead of creating a new one"

Fetches (WebFetch): F1 support.apple.com/103769; F2 bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=41419; F3 rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6265#section-8.5; F4 rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455#section-4.1; F5 developer.mozilla.org Crypto/randomUUID; F6 w3.org/TR/secure-contexts; F7 websockets.spec.whatwg.org; F8 developer.apple.com/forums/thread/70139 (IP SAN, DTS, lead only); F9 cheatsheetseries.owasp.org WebSocket_Security; F10 developer.apple.com/forums/thread/104488; F11 docs.rs/rcgen KeyPair; F12 support.apple.com/102390; F13 html.spec.whatwg.org nav-history-apis (the replaceState text was past the first 100k characters and was not read; Q15 stands in).
